blocks.soundsLike: GET ONE'S NICKERS IN A TWIST
blocks.note: nicker is British slang for a pound; you put your pounds in the pot when you twist, taking another card in pontoon

explanation.surface: A card player puts more money in the pot and then loses their nerve.
explanation.walkthrough: Knickers are British for women's underpants, and 'nicker' is slang for a pound, so the two sound alike. In pontoon, a British card game, 'twist' asks for another card.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: British slang for getting flustered and upset over something minor.

clue.text: Recording short, easy putt (3-2)

indicators.note: a word that is short falls short of its end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: taping is recording, and it loses its G

explanation.surface: A golfer films a short, easy putt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short, easy putt' reads as one description; short belongs with recording and cuts it.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: a putt so close to the hole that it needs only a tap.

clue.text: Not one retailer stocks chemical for photocopier (5)

indicators.note: a shop that stocks something holds it inside, so the words hold the answer

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of not to the start of retailer

explanation.surface: No shop stocks the powder a photocopier needs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stocks' looks like a shop's inventory, fitting the retailer; it is the hiding instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: the powdered ink a photocopier fuses onto paper.

clue.text: Obsessive desire to publish in mostly kind country having run away (9)

indicators.note: mostly means all but a little, so the last letter goes
the R for run has run away, leaving the word

blocks.note: TYPE, a kind, without its last letter
the European country
R = run, as in cricket scoring; it leaves the country

explanation.surface: A compulsive writer craves to publish in a kinder country, after fleeing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run away' reads as fleeing; it tells you R has gone from ROMANIA.
explanation.definitionFit: A formed word: -mania is a craze, and typo- means type, so a craze for seeing oneself in print.

clue.text: Japanese coin found in Argyll and Bute town close to Clachaig (5)

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its last letter

blocks.note: Oban, a port town on the west coast of Scotland
the last letter of Clachaig

explanation.surface: A Japanese coin turns up in a Scottish town near Clachaig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as near, and Clachaig is a real place in Argyll; it means the close, or end, of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: this large oval gold piece of old Japan is a coin.

clue.text: Ship is grand the whole time (7)

blocks.note: G = grand, a thousand pounds
all = the whole
an eon is a long time

explanation.surface: A ship is looking grand all the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The whole time' reads as one phrase meaning always, and 'grand' as splendid; a grand is slang for a thousand pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the big square-rigged sailing vessel of Spain's treasure fleets is one kind of ship.

clue.text: Fight arrest (3,2)

blocks.note: a quarrel or clash, as in 'a brush with the law'
police slang for taking a suspect to the station

explanation.surface: Someone resists arrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fight arrest' reads as resisting the police; the two words are separate definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a noun for a clash or quarrel, and a phrasal verb for taking someone into custody.

clue.text: Scoff too much? Partner scratching head before repast, off and on (7)

indicators.note: to scratch something out is to strike it, so the head, the first letter, goes
off and on means intermittently, so letters are skipped and kept in turn

blocks.note: LOVER without its first letter
the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of repast

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether they eat too much, while their partner scratches their head over a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoff' reads as mock; it is British slang for eating greedily.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang sense: scoff means gobble, so doing it to excess is eating too much.

clue.text: I rate Chas & Dave finally breaking rubbish flower (9)

definitions.note: the definition is what this taster might say of the job: cha is slang for tea

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so the last letter
the E breaks into the rubbish, sitting inside it

blocks.note: tat is junk
the last letter of Dave; it breaks into the rubbish
an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: A fan rates the Cockney duo Chas & Dave, while calling their flowers rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Chas & Dave were a Cockney pop duo; 'Chas' here is the plural of cha, slang for tea, so the whole of 'I rate Chas' is what a tea taster says.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: someone paid to grade teas could say 'I rate chas'.
